[[File:Lifeism in Lifeist Script.png|thumb|Lifeism in Lifeist Script]]
'''The Lifeist script''' is a logographic block script for writing English.  
It is designed to make English functionally logographic while preserving the arbitrariness, historical depth, and etymological structure of English spelling.<ref name=":0">https://chatgpt.com/c/6917d611-56e8-8330-b087-4b71dc4a521f</ref>

Most English spelling reforms are proposed to make English more phonetic. They prioritize the pronounciation of a specific region over others, generally General American pronounciation. And they hide the etymology of English words, and as a result the history of the language.<ref name=":0" />

The Lifeist script is an attempt at English spelling reform to do the opposite. The Lifest script seeks to do the exact opposite. It seeks to represent the meanings of English words through creating syllabic blocks from the current English spellings. These syllabic blocks may be interpreted as being similar to Hangul, the Korean script that is used to write Korean, but the intention behind them is fundamentally different. Hangul is very regular in its spelling. The irregularities that exist in Hangul are irregularities that simply emerged from recent phonological shifts. By contrast, the Lifest script is designed to turn English syllables into logograms that are identifiable by all speakers, or rather all English readers, regardless of what their dialect is. They do not include pronunciation except for the fact that the syllable count is marked. In the future, when English has more phonological shifts, such as possibly erosion of consonant clusters and the development of tones, the Lifest characters will still maintain their semantic meaning as representing the word that was inherited from English of the 21st century and, by extension, wherever it may have come from before. The Lifest script is intended to not prioritize any regions over other regions, because English is not something that belongs to just one group. English is a language that represents a common heritage of over a billion people in the world with vastly different backgrounds who speak in vastly different ways.<ref name=":0" /> 

== Principles ==

=== 1. Every English word is divided into syllabic blocks ===
Lifeist Script is a block-based writing system.  
Each written unit (a ''block'') is a ''pseudo-syllable'' derived from English spelling rather than from English phonology.

A block generally contains:
* an optional onset
* a vowel nucleus
* an optional coda

These are orthographic units, not linguistic syllables.

=== 2. Block division follows English orthography, not phonology ===
Lifeist Script does ''not'' attempt to represent spoken English syllables.  
Instead, block segmentation follows:
* English spelling  
* English morphology  
* historical etymological structures  
* standard orthographic clusters  

This preserves the depth and irregularity of English, rather than simplifying it.

=== 3. Double consonants in spelling are written as double codas ===
If English spelling contains a doubled consonant (''nn, tt, pp, ll, ss''), the first block absorbs both consonants into its coda.

Examples:
* ''dinner'' → '''DINN''' + '''ER'''
* ''diner'' → '''DIN''' + '''ER'''
* ''bitter'' → '''BITT''' + '''ER'''
* ''biter'' → '''BIT''' + '''ER'''
* ''dipper'' → '''DIPP''' + '''ER'''
* ''seppuku'' → '''SEPP''' + '''PU''' + '''KU'''

This preserves all orthographic distinctions without introducing phonemic gemination that English does not naturally possess.

Dipper will probably be simplified to '''DIP''' + '''ER''' by later speakers but in our rules that is how it goes

=== 3.1. Consonants can be spread across coda and initial of next syllable ===
Consonants can be spread across the coda and the initial of the next syllable

* ''battery'' → '''BATT''' + '''TER''' + '''Y'''
* ''seppuku'' → '''SEPP''' + '''PU''' + '''KU'''
* ''natural'' → '''NAT''' + '''TUR''' + '''AL'''
* ''national'' → '''NAT''' + '''TION''' + '''AL'''
* ''natal'' → '''NAT''' + '''AL'''
** Not an example but demonstrates how -al is considered a common enough suffix to not warrant an initial
* ''racial'' → '''RAC''' + '''IAL'''

If it is doubled in the first consonant then there are two of the consonant in the English spelling, even though there are three here

This happens if the syllables and their pronounciations are somehow unique and information is preserved of the syllable by doing so

=== 4. Consonants are not doubled unless spelling doubles them ===
Overlapping consonants at block boundaries (coda → onset) do ''not'' create new doubling.

Examples:
* ''natural'' → '''NAT''' + '''TUR''' + '''AL'''
* ''battery'' → '''BATT''' + '''TER''' + '''Y'''

Even when phonology might allow a geminate, the script only doubles where English spelling doubles.

=== 5. Coda consonants may optionally reappear as onset consonants ===
When a consonant ends one block and begins the next, writers may use either:
* '''clean separation''' (coda appears once), or
* '''overlap style''' (coda also visually repeats as onset)

Both are valid stylistic variants and do not change meaning.

=== 6. Ruby pronunciation guides are optional ===
Ruby characters (placed above the block) may be used to indicate pronunciation.  
These:
* may vary by dialect  
* are pedagogical tools  
* are not part of the block identity  
* can vanish over time without affecting literacy

=== 7. Determinatives are used only for overloaded blocks ===
Determinatives are small semantic markers added ''only'' when a pseudo-syllable:
* is highly overloaded with unrelated meanings  
* has unstable pronunciation across dialects  
* collapses many different morphemes into one ambiguous form  

Examples of candidates:
* '''TU''' (to/too/two)  
* '''AN''' (article vs. suffix)  
* '''US''' (Latin ''-us'' vs. pronoun ''us'')

Determinatives are ''not'' used for:
* common function words  
* universally understood syllables  
* clearly differentiated forms  

They are rare and introduced only when ambiguity obstructs logographic identity.

=== 8. Acronyms remain alphabetic ===
Initialisms and acronyms do not use blocks.

Examples:
* '''FBI'''
* '''NHK'''
* '''LGBTQ'''

Alphabetic forms are preserved for clarity and tradition.

=== 9. Vowel nuclei follow English spelling ===
Lifeist Script records the orthographic vowel, not the phonetic one.

Examples:
* ''ea'' stays '''EA'''
* ''igh'' stays '''IGH'''
* ''oo'' stays '''OO'''
* ''ou'' stays '''OU'''

This preserves English etymological depth.

=== 10. Syllable boundaries follow spelling and morphology ===
Morphological and etymological divisions determine block boundaries.

Examples:
* ''national'' → '''NAT''' + '''ION''' + '''AL'''
* ''cactus'' → '''CAC''' + '''TUS'''
* ''illegal'' → '''IL''' + '''LEGAL'''

Lifeist Script prioritizes written structure over spoken form.

=== 11. The script is not intended to simplify English ===
Lifeist Script:
* preserves irregularity  
* celebrates historical complexity  
* resists phonetic reduction  
* remains stable across future sound changes  
* emphasizes symbolic and aesthetic depth rather than efficiency  

The script is intentionally non-phonocentric.

=== 12. The script embodies Lifeist metaphysics ===
The block structure symbolically encodes:
* unity through coda–onset overlaps  
* historical layering within the self  
* the metaphysical movement from ''ara-mitama'' to ''kushi-mitama''  
* the beauty of arbitrary forms  
* the sacredness of linguistic and personal history  

Lifeist Script is both a practical writing system and an esoteric expression of Lifeism.
